newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco attorney says memo was frivolous marketing ploy.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco attorney says memo was frivolous marketing ploy.

text.p: An alleged tobacco industry memo suggesting a foul-tasting cigarette be marketed to rebellious teen-agers was a "frivolous attempt" by unknown marketing people to find another way to sell cigarettes, a tobacco company attorney said on Thursday.

The purported British American Tobacco Co. memorandum was introduced by the state of Florida late Wednesday in its $1 billion lawsuit that seeks to recover the costs of treating sick smokers. It was part of a motion seeking release of still-private tobacco documents the state claims will show the industry targeted teen smokers.

"The whole idea is bizarre. It was an idea that came from marketing people that went absolutely nowhere," said the tobacco company's attorney, David Bernick, when asked about the two-page handwritten memo that suggested it market a cigarette treated with ammonia to make it more addictive.
The memo was introduced by attorneys for Florida during a hearing before Special Master William Rutter on Wednesday.
In the memo, the unidentified author suggests that British American market an "unconventional" cigarette that could appeal to rebellious youth but not their parents.
"It would respond to the person's individuality with the possibility of being an alternative to drugs," the writer said.

The cigarette should "incorporate some sort of 'kick' of a similar nature to the Coca-Cola 'kick', giving the cigarette a physiological effect," the writer added, explaining that this might be accomplished by using ammonia to liberate more nicotine from tobacco and enhance the effect of the nicotine.
The writer said the "flavors would be new and unconventional, and probably foul-tasting to the average smoker." The flavors discussed as possible additives were "Root Beer and Brazilian Fruit Juice."

The writer said the idea was discussed during a meeting in which it was felt that the foul taste would help marketing. "It was felt that the rebellion aspect would be encouraged if the cigarette ... tasted horribly," the memo said.
Wayne Hogan, one of Florida's attorneys, said the memo was "another smoking gun" supporting the state's allegation that the tobacco industry did target teen-agers.
"This issue was discussed in depth, and indicates that it was a project that had been discussed in depth," he said.
However, Bernick, said production of such a cigarette would have discouraged teen smoking.

He said the memo, which was not written on British American letterhead, came from company files but said he was not sure it was a company document. The tobacco company gave Florida the memo as part of a group of documents months ago.
